qc_3_droite.blurb: Droite is the right-hand sector of the Gros Bonnet cliff in the Vallée du Bras-du-Nord, in the Portneuf region of Quebec. A broad slab that stacks up many pitches steepens into a vertical headwall near the top. The eleven lines are almost all traditional, with one that mixes in some aid. Grades start around 5.6 and reach a single 5.12, but most sit between 5.10 and 5.11. Some of the routes run nine pitches, so plan a full day rather than a quick visit. The descent is a pleasant walk-off on a trail, and the river beside the road is handy for cooling off afterward.

qc_forebay.blurb: Forebay is a single bouldering block beside the river in Alma, on the Lac-Saint-Jean side of the Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean region, upstream of a dam. It stands roughly five metres tall and carries twelve problems. Most fall between V1 and V4, with a couple of harder ones and a single V6, so there is something for a range of levels. The block was cleaned in 2023 and is still being developed. A trail drops from the end of a residential street in town down to the water, passing a viewpoint and a small stream before the boulder comes into view.

qc_le_paradis.blurb: Le Paradis is a well-hidden cliff of impressive size near L'Anse-Saint-Jean in the Saguenay region. Twelve routes mix traditional and sport lines, and a few are multi-pitch. The wall is described as vertical and lovely, and a small pond nearby gives a place to cool off between climbs in summer. Grades run from the 5.8 range to the low 5.12s, with the largest group at 5.11, so it leans toward experienced leaders rather than beginners. The trail in from the roadside parking is short.

qc_lac_blanc_main_cliff.blurb: The main cliff at Lac Blanc stands above the east shore of the lake in the Lanaudière region, in the Forêt Ouareau area. A prominent arête rises from a flat terrace at its base. It holds twelve routes, seven traditional and five sport, ranging from about 5.7 up to a lone 5.12. Most are in the 5.8 and 5.10 range. The wall faces southwest, so it sees early shade and then sun for the rest of the day, and the position above the water brings a breeze on hot afternoons. The area has a reputation for staying quiet.
qc_lac_blanc_main_cliff.approach: A trail of about 2 km leads from the roadside parking area to the cliff, roughly 15 to 20 minutes on foot, ending at the flat terrace below the wall.

qc_g_champs_lys_es.blurb: Champs-Élysées is a sector of Mont-Césaire at Val-David in the Laurentides, a hill that is popular with school groups. The wall is about 20 metres tall, vertical to overhanging, and faces west. It dries quickly and suits hot summer days. Eleven routes are mostly traditional, with a couple of sport lines, and they span the easy 5.6 range up to around 5.12, with a good cluster at 5.9 and 5.11. This is the part of the mountain with the most concentrated hard climbing, so it fits intermediate and advanced climbers. Most anchors are trees.

qc_06_le_cerveau.blurb: Le Cerveau is a large block set apart from the main face at L'Amphithéâtre, a quartzite cliff at Saint-André-de-Kamouraska in the Bas-Saint-Laurent region. Its brain-like shape gives it the name. Eleven routes are split between seven sport lines and four top-rope lines, running from about 5.7 to 5.11 with the biggest group at 5.10. The wider crag is sport only and can get crowded on weekends. You can reach the block by a short link from the lower part of a neighbouring sector, or from the trail along the top, which involves some scrambling down.
